data.title: Why China’s AI giants spend far less and still shrink compute gap with US rivals
data.description:
The massive gap in artificial intelligence spending between US and Chinese tech titans may not buy the advantage expected for American giants, as lower domestic costs and heavy state support allow Chinese firms to secure far more computing power per dollar, according to a new report by Moody’s Ratings.
While US hyperscalers outspent their Chinese counterparts by a staggering margin, the physical gap in computing capacity was nowhere near as wide as those mega-budgets suggested, the report said.
Lower buildout costs, targeted policy incentives and access to cheaper green energy meant Chinese tech firms were punching above their financial weight, narrowing the compute divide with American peers at a fraction of the price, Moody’s noted.
The US retained a clear overall lead in cutting-edge semiconductor chips, but the findings suggested headline capex numbers tell only part of the story. Here is what you need to know.
How wide is the spending gap between US and Chinese tech giants?
Capital expenditure by China’s major tech companies was set to more than double to around US$140 billion this year – up from US$65 billion in 2025 – and reach US$165 billion by 2027, according to Moody’s.
By contrast, five major US hyperscalers – Microsoft, Amazon Web Services, Alphabet, Meta Platforms and Oracle – plus AI cloud provider CoreWeave were projected to spend more than US$785 billion this year alone, approaching US$1 trillion by 2027.

Why does China’s AI infrastructure cost so much less?
China’s cost advantage lies in land, power and structural state backing.
Under Beijing’s “East Data, West Computing” initiative, power-intensive workloads are routed to resource-rich inland regions like Inner Mongolia and the northwestern province of Gansu.
By moving latency-tolerant AI training to hubs with abundant green energy and cooler climates – such as ByteDance’s expanding data centre footprint in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia – companies could slash power and cooling expenses while reserving valuable coastal capacity for real-time applications, according to BMI, a Fitch Solutions company.
Government policy further tilted the scales through cheaper infrastructure, subsidies, fast-tracked approvals, and tax incentives, according to Moody’s.
What is holding China back from overtaking the US?
China’s cost advantage is concentrated mainly in non-chip infrastructure.
Servers and accelerators accounted for the largest share of AI spending, while restricted access to leading-edge Nvidia chips remained a key constraint, Moody’s said. Domestic processors and software ecosystems continued to improve but still lagged Nvidia’s.
There is also an efficiency trade-off. BMI said some Chinese semiconductor platforms consumed more electricity than Nvidia processors to perform equivalent computing workloads, meaning cheaper power and subsidies could only partly offset the higher operating costs of domestic hardware.
At the system level, the trade-off is also stark. Semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis estimated that Huawei Technologies’ CloudMatrix 384 drew about 4.1 times as much power as Nvidia’s GB200 NVL72, while delivering nearly twice the computing performance, making access to abundant and relatively cheap electricity particularly important.
Is China actually closing the compute gap?
Measured by data centre capacity rather than pure dollar spend, the divide shrinks significantly.
Installed US data centre capacity stood at 52 gigawatts (GW) at the end of 2025, compared with 28GW in China, according to International Energy Agency figures cited by Moody’s.
By 2030, US capacity was forecast to reach 100GW, compared with 67GW in China. China’s capacity was expected to grow at an annual rate of 19 per cent, faster than the US rate of 14 per cent, narrowing the relative gap even as the absolute difference increased.




While megawatt output does not directly equate to AI processing power, it shows that the capex gap overstates the physical capacity divide. China’s faster growth rate means it is steadily narrowing the relative gap even as the absolute difference expands.
Model capabilities reflect this catch-up. Leading Chinese models – including Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, Z.ai’s GLM-5.3, and Alibaba Group Holding’s Qwen3.8 – now rank alongside top global open-weight rivals on benchmark platforms like Artificial Analysis and Chatbot Arena.
Can Chinese tech giants turn these AI gains into revenue?
Building compute is one thing; monetising it is another.
Cloud platforms remained the main engine for AI revenue, but Chinese hyperscalers operated at a much smaller scale and in a more price-competitive market, Moody’s said.
In their latest reported quarters, Microsoft generated US$59 billion in cloud revenue, Amazon US$42 billion, and Alphabet US$25 billion. Alibaba generated US$7 billion and Baidu about US$1 billion.
US hyperscalers also benefited from larger enterprise customer bases, contracted cloud commitments and integrated software ecosystems, giving them clearer paths to recurring AI revenue. China’s lower-cost open-source models were driving adoption, but monetisation remained at an earlier stage, Moody’s said.
There are signs the gap is beginning to narrow. Alibaba’s cloud business reported 45 per cent revenue growth in the June quarter – the fastest pace in 22 quarters – as demand for AI-related products accelerated.
Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

data.title: China pumps massive US$54b into insurers, banks in financial powerhouse push
data.description:
China rolled out a package of capital injections worth about 360 billion yuan (US$54 billion) on Sunday for the country’s largest state-owned insurers and state banks, marking a step towards Beijing’s long-flagged plan to build itself into a global financial powerhouse.
The Ministry of Finance, which led the move, had rarely injected capital into financial institutions at such magnitude, according to analysts.
China Life Insurance Company said it would receive 35 billion yuan to help strengthen its “ability to withstand risk”, according to its website.
Among banks, the Agricultural Bank of China planned to raise up to 160 billion yuan through a private placement of new A shares to the finance ministry, China National Tobacco Corporation and related subsidiaries, an exchange filing showed.
Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) was targeting up to 100 billion yuan from the same group of investors, according to an exchange filing.
Recent top-level meetings have all called for more proactive fiscal policy to counter growth pressures, and capital injections into financial institutions are part of that fiscal toolkit
Shen Meng, Chanson & Co
The Export-Import Bank of China, a policy lender known as Eximbank, was set to receive 30 billion yuan to “significantly enhance its capacity to support the real economy and opening up, while reinforcing its resilience in risk prevention”, according to state news agency Xinhua.
The People’s Insurance Company (Group) of China planned to issue new shares in onshore markets to raise as much as 15 billion yuan, with the finance ministry subscribing in cash, according to its filing with the Shanghai exchange on Sunday.
China Export & Credit Insurance Corporation, known as Sinosure, announced a 10 billion yuan injection to replenish its core capital, aimed at improving its solvency adequacy ratio and expanding its capacity to meet insurance obligations.
China Taiping Insurance Group was set to receive 7 billion yuan to help it withstand risk, according to the company’s website.
China Reinsurance planned to issue new A shares, with the finance ministry set to subscribe in cash for a total of 3 billion yuan, according to its filing with the Hong Kong stock exchange.
“Recent top-level meetings have all called for more proactive fiscal policy to counter growth pressures, and capital injections into financial institutions are part of that fiscal toolkit,” said Shen Meng, a director at Beijing-based investment firm Chanson & Co.
“They not only reduce operational and regulatory risks for these institutions, but also stimulate broader investment and consumption through the multiplier effect of the financial sector.”
Shen said the finance ministry had “rarely injected capital into financial institutions on such a scale, and that the few precedents were mainly aimed at repairing balance sheets and cutting risk”.
The capital injections build on Beijing’s ambition to transform China into a financial powerhouse, a goal the central bank formally embedded in its first-ever stand-alone five-year plan this year, which pledges to expand the yuan’s global use and build a “strong central bank” to drive that vision.
S&P Global Ratings has estimated China’s big four state-owned banks – ICBC, China Construction Bank, Agricultural Bank of China and Bank of China – faced a capital shortfall of as much as 3.7 trillion yuan by 2025 to meet total loss-absorbing capacity (TLAC) requirements.
TLAC refers to a capital buffer international regulators require of the world’s biggest banks so they can absorb losses in a crisis without needing a government bailout.
China’s six largest state-owned banks posted their first simultaneous increase in both first-half revenue and net profit since 2022 this year, driven by a tentative recovery in net interest margins – the gap between what banks earn on loans and pay out on deposits.
That margin had steadily narrowed over the previous two years, dragging the industry average down to a record low of nearly 1.4 per cent in the first quarter of 2026.
Beijing’s push to fortify its state financial institutions dovetails with efforts to elevate Hong Kong’s role.
Regulators have urged mainland insurers to invest in Hong Kong-listed exchange-traded funds (ETFs), bolstering the city’s status as a global financial centre.
Ping An, the country’s largest private insurer, had sought regulatory approval to expand into Hong Kong ETFs after posting 36 per cent profit growth in the first half of this year, according to the company’s board secretary.
Mainland financial firms are also ramping up overseas fundraising to support yuan internationalisation. Last year alone, companies including China Pacific Insurance, ICBC and China Everbright Bank each raised between US$300 million and US$2 billion in Hong Kong and other offshore markets.

data.title: ‘A victim’: American Bully dies in surgery, owners question fighting dog rules
data.description:
The owners of an American Bully are challenging the authorities’ classification of “fighting dogs” after their pet, a breed strictly controlled in Hong Kong, died during neutering, a procedure they undertook amid a crackdown on non-compliance.
Monchiu, a female, died under anaesthesia during the operation at a veterinary clinic on Friday, her owners said on social media late on Saturday.
They said the dog, who suffered from vision and hearing impairment, as well as skin problems, was unfit for surgery but they proceeded out of fear she might be taken into the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department’s custody.
The owners said the dog had been repeatedly reported since authorities stepped up checks, although they insisted she was obedient and posed no threat.
“We were very afraid that it would be reported and taken to the department for detention. It had physical defects – it was born blind in one eye and could not hear, and had skin problems – and she could not survive such hot weather in the detention cell,” said the owners, who called themselves “dad and mum”.
“Monchiu is a victim under the indiscriminate law enforcement of the department.”
They questioned the classification of fighting dogs.
“We hope that the departure of Monchiu could fight for the vindication and rectification of other Bullies in Hong Kong – Bully dogs are not fighting dogs and it is extremely risky for them to undergo forced sterilisation surgery,” they said.
Concerns over the management of large and fighting dogs grew in Hong Kong after two attacks in mid-August.
In the first incident, on August 17, two small dogs were mauled to death by a 60kg dog with genetic links to a mastiff in Yuen Long town centre.
Days later, a 33-year-old woman was found dead near her pet training centre in Ta Kwu Ling after being attacked by a 30kg dog with traits associated with pit bull ancestry.

Under Hong Kong law, four types of “fighting dogs”, the pit bull terrier, dogo Argentino, Japanese Tosa and fila Brasileiro, and their crossbreeds are banned from import or local breeding.
They must be securely muzzled, kept on a leash no longer than 1.5 metres and wear a special collar when in public. Existing fighting dogs must also be neutered to be kept legally.
The attacks prompted authorities to review the definitions of fighting dogs, and the department has strengthened inspection and enforcement.
At least three dogs have been detained by the department on suspicion of being fighting dogs.
On Wednesday, the department said the American Bully, alongside the American pit bull terrier and American Staffordshire terrier, was classified under pit bull terriers and therefore subject to fighting dog regulations.
The department said the law regulated by “type” rather than “breed” and the three breeds had long been regarded as falling under the pit bull terrier type.
It added that the three breeds had always been subject to the same strict regulations, and that the policy and definition of fighting dogs had not changed.
In response to Monchiu’s case, the department said on Sunday that it had not received any inquiry or report concerning the animal, and had not classified it as a fighting dog.
It said the determination of fighting dog types was the responsibility of the department’s veterinary officers, who would carefully observe the dog’s physical characteristics and external proportions, body structure, and related features to assess whether the dog truly possessed the high-risk traits characteristic of the fighting dog types, and thereby classify the dog.
“This is the common international practice for identifying fighting dog types,” it said.
The department said that if a classified fighting dog had not been desexed, it would escort the animal to a private veterinary clinic appointed by the dog keeper for desexing surgery.
“The appointed private veterinarian will carry out a medical examination of the dog. If, on medical grounds, the veterinarian considers the dog unfit for surgery, a direction will be issued to the dog keeper allowing the surgery to be postponed until the dog’s health has been restored,” a department spokesman said.
The department urged keepers to consult a registered vet before subjecting their dogs to any surgical procedures. Those who were worried that their pets could be fighting dogs should contact the department or a registered vet for verification, it said.
The department also said that citywide special inspection and enforcement operations on the proper control of dogs on August 30 and this weekend had found three suspected cases where large dogs were not being securely held on a leash in public places.
It added that its officers would follow up on these cases and institute prosecutions accordingly.

data.title: Why Chelsea football shirts are making Hong Kong fans nervous about crypto laws
data.description:
English Premier League football club Chelsea’s lucrative new front-of-shirt sponsorship deal with a stablecoin issuer has left Hong Kong fans and retailers concerned about whether wearing or selling the top counts as illegal promotion under digital currency laws.
Chelsea signed the deal with Circle to feature its USDC stablecoin brand on player jerseys for the 2026-27 season in late August, just three months after the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) warned Premier League clubs about partnering with unauthorised crypto and finance businesses.
Circle’s UK arm, Circle UK Trading, is an FCA-regulated company providing certain financial services. But USDC is not issued or regulated under the laws of the United Kingdom, nor is it distributed by a licensed stablecoin issuer in Hong Kong.
Only two stablecoin issuers are currently licensed in Hong Kong – Anchorpoint Financial Limited and HSBC.
Ahead of the enactment of the Stablecoins Ordinance on August 1, 2025, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) warned on its website that “it will be illegal for any person to … actively market the issue of unlicensed [fiat-referenced stablecoins] to the public”.
Winnie Choi, a Chelsea fan of 12 years, was among those worried about breaking the law.
“After looking up the law, I still do not understand whether it is a problem to wear the jersey,” she said.
Choi suggested that the HKMA issue a clear, “down-to-earth” guideline on whether wearing the shirt with the USDC logo constituted promotion.
Danny*, a club supporter for more than 20 years, said ordinary football fans would not have the awareness to identify if the shirt promoted an unregulated stablecoin.
“If I wear it, who will enforce the law? Will I be arrested by police?” he said.
Danny said he would not buy the new jersey until authorities clarified whether it was legal to wear it.

Hammer Chung, owner of football apparel shop DirectSoccer in Mong Kok, said he was unsure whether it was legal to sell replica jerseys with the USDC logo.
He added that he hoped regulators would clarify the matter.
But Chung noted that many of the kits for other football clubs that he sold also bore the logos of illegal gambling websites.
“Are we also promoting for them by selling the shirts?” he said.
The HKMA said it would not comment on individual cases, but noted the ordinance prohibited the “active marketing” or advertising of unauthorised stablecoin activity in Hong Kong.
Whether an act constituted actively marketing to the public was determined on a case-by-case basis, a spokesman said.
Factors considered by the HKMA included the languages used in the marketing messages, whether they targeted people living in the city, whether a Hong Kong domain name was used and whether a detailed marketing plan was in place to promote the activity.
A specific exemption was provided to publishers and live broadcasters who merely published content created by others, as long as they satisfied the relevant conditions set out in the provision and considered the relevant facts and circumstances, he said.

Blockchain expert Louis Li Sze-chung expressed concerns that fans donning the new Chelsea shirt in public could be “problematic”, as it all depended on how the HKMA defined active marketing.
“There are so many grey areas,” he said, adding that he dared not wear T-shirts sporting the logos of unlicensed crypto trading platforms after the licensing regime was put in place by the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC).
Li said USDC was the second-largest stablecoin in the world, and it was ridiculous that it was labelled as “unlicensed” under local legislation.
He also said it was difficult to regulate the promotion of cryptocurrencies within a certain jurisdiction in the age of the internet because they were issued globally. “How can you say something legal in other countries is illegal here?”
The ordinance provides an exemption for promoting unlicensed stablecoins across various media and digital platforms, including live broadcasts, provided the person did not devise and exercised no control over the content of the advertisement.
“A group of players on TV is wearing [shirts with] this logo … it’s impossible that it isn’t an advertisement. We’re looking at them the entire game, right?” Li said.


Tanna Chong, head of public policy at VerifyVASP, a digital assets compliance company, called for enhanced consumer protection through disclaimers before every match, similar to warning messages in moneylending advertisements.
“They would be clear reminders that the programme contains these materials [about cryptocurrency], and that those companies actually do not have a licence in Hong Kong,” she said.
Chong, who helped draft the ordinance during her time in government, said there was no hard and fast rule to define active marketing, noting that it was a concept determined on a case-by-case basis considering various contextual factors.
She said neither Circle nor Chelsea had control over the broadcasting of matches in Hong Kong, which involved a deal between NowTV and the Premier League, and had not actively implemented a marketing campaign in the city.
Circle was not “by way of business providing services” in the city either, she added.
She also reassured fans that there was no problem with wearing the Blues’ shirt with the USDC logo, as wearers were not the service provider.
“Unless [the wearer] is a Circle employee walking down the street in a Chelsea jersey. In that case, you need to establish that Circle instructed him to wear it with the intent of targeting a Hong Kong audience,” she said.
An HKT spokesman said Now TV strictly complied with all relevant Hong Kong laws and regulations.
The South China Morning Post has reached out to Circle and Chelsea FC for comment.
The West London club’s latest deal followed a collective agreement by all 20 Premier League clubs to phase out front-of-shirt gambling sponsors. But the Blues are not the first team to partner with the crypto sector.

OKX and Kraken, both virtual asset trading platforms unlicensed in Hong Kong, are the sleeve sponsors of Manchester City and Tottenham Hotspur.
Chelsea itself also partnered with crypto platform BingX, which is also unlicensed in Hong Kong, for an official training kit front sponsorship.
During their visit to the city last month, Chelsea players wore the training kit with the BingX logo during an open training session at Kai Tak Stadium.
Players from City and Spurs also wore kits sporting the OKX and Kraken logos during their friendlies in Hong Kong in August this year and July last year, respectively.
Similar clauses regulating the promotion of unlicensed virtual asset trading platforms are present in the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance.
The SFC said it would not comment on specific cases. It added that it would take into account all marketing and advertising activities in their totality in considering the appropriate course of action.
Kraken said that it maintained jurisdiction-specific controls designed to ensure its activities complied with applicable local laws.
The trading platform also stressed that its partnership with Tottenham Hotspur was a global brand sponsorship.
It did not reflect an offer, solicitation or promotion of Kraken’s virtual asset trading services in jurisdictions where those activities were restricted, it added.
The SCMP has reached out to Manchester City, OKX, Tottenham Hotspur and BingX for comment.
*Name changed at interviewee’s request.

data.title: Huawei’s Tau Scaling Law chip overcomes overheating hurdle, paper shows
data.description:
Huawei Technologies has released a new research paper showing its Tau Scaling Law-based semiconductor architecture can avoid overheating, which analysts view as a key technical hurdle for its anticipated Kirin 2026 smartphone chip.
The paper, authored by He Tingbo, chairwoman of the Huawei Scientist Committee and president of the company’s semiconductor business department, rebutted scepticism that vertically stacking logic circuits would create an insurmountable thermal bottleneck.
It was published on Friday on ChinaXiv, a publication platform for scientific papers that have yet to be peer reviewed.
Despite heat being “the sharpest concern on Tau Scaling Law”, the company’s measurements for its new Kirin chip “turned that objection upside down”, He wrote.
The paper said the Kirin 2026 chip ran cooler than its predecessor, while packing 55 per cent more transistors per square millimetre and cutting power use by up to 66 per cent on some key tasks.
The new chip reduces power consumption while increasing transistor density, allowing it to flexibly switch between functional constraints and peak performance
Kaiyuan Securities
The new chip reduces power consumption while increasing transistor density, allowing it to flexibly switch between functional constraints and peak performance
By vertically stacking active chip tiers, the design drastically shortened the physical distance that data signals must travel, cutting energy waste across neural processing units, graphics processing units, central processing units and digital signal processors – modules that dominate a smartphone chip’s thermal budget, the paper said. It also significantly boosted transistor density over last year’s Kirin 9030 Pro.
Analysts said the findings guarantee performance for the coming launch of Huawei’s next flagship Mate series smartphones.
In a research note to clients on Saturday, domestic brokerage Kaiyuan Securities said the new architecture balanced raw performance with power savings.
Kaiyuan analysts said Huawei tackled this in two ways: it reduced source power density through folding to prevent localised high temperatures, while actively managing thermal layout during design by placing the most heat-intensive modules in positions with the clearest heat dissipation paths to achieve balance.
“The new chip reduces power consumption while increasing transistor density, allowing it to flexibly switch between functional constraints and peak performance,” they said.
Zheng Lei, chief economist at Samoyed Cloud Technology Group, said the method was “born out of necessity”, based on Huawei’s projections for its chip performance.
While this method had limits, there was room for development, Zheng said, adding he believed the new Kirin chip would successfully resolve its overheating issues using this method.
The paper is Huawei’s third since unveiling its Tau Scaling Law in May.
The theoretical framework, presented by He, claimed its LogicFolding architecture could achieve transistor densities equivalent to the cutting-edge 1.4-nanometre processes by 2031 without access to advanced extreme ultraviolet lithography machines banned for sale in China due to US sanctions.
In a second paper published in July, the company said its coming smartphone processor was on track for a 55 per cent density boost over the Kirin 9030 Pro, based on new production data.
Analysts also expected Huawei’s progress on heat management to ripple across a few domestic players who could also potentially help Huawei address the thermal issues.
Kaiyuan Securities suggested focusing on directions such as fabs, chip packaging and testing, and new chip equipment.
Zhang Xinyuan, an analyst from Beijing-based think tank Kefangde, said the principle could spur innovations in areas such as new semiconductor materials and 3D heterogeneous integration technologies.
